summary: This document specifies a DHCPv6 option for exchanging information about a client's fully qualified domain name and about who is responsible for updating the DNS resource records related to the client's address assignments.

plainLanguage.summary: A computer using the newer address style can ask for a name and agree with the server about who writes it in the DNS phone book.

questions: what is the dhcpv6 client fqdn option
what do the s o and n flags mean in dhcpv6 fqdn
subtitle: How a DHCPv6 client and server agree on the client's DNS name and on who updates the DNS records.

tldr.problem: When a host gets an IPv6 address from a DHCPv6 server, the DNS records that map its name to the address (AAAA) and the address back to the name (PTR) need updating. Nothing told client and server who does which update or what the name is.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 4704 defines the Client FQDN option (code 39). It carries the client's full or partial domain name plus three flag bits (S, O and N) that the client and server use to negotiate who updates the AAAA and PTR records.
tldr.outcome: Sites keep full control through local policy. The server always handles the PTR record, and either the client or the server handles the AAAA record, or the client asks for no server updates at all.

Suggested record TTL

today: RFC 4704 is a Proposed Standard published in October 2006. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Names and Addresses in DNS
sections.content:
DNS keeps the mapping between a host's Fully Qualified Domain Name (FQDN) and its IPv6 addresses in two kinds of resource record: AAAA (name to address) and PTR (address to name). The DNS update specification, RFC 2136, lets those records be changed over the network.

DHCPv6 (RFC 3315) hands a client its stateful IPv6 addresses. RFC 4704 adds a new DHCPv6 option, the Client FQDN option, so that the client and server can exchange the client's name and agree on who is responsible for the DNS updates.
sections.plainLanguage: A DNS record is like an entry in a phone book. This document lets a computer and its helper agree on what name goes in the book and who writes it.

sections.title: Who Updates What
sections.content:
Getting an address can trigger two separate DNS updates: one for the AAAA record and one for the PTR record. In principle the client and the server could each do none, one or both, but the RFC says only two arrangements really make sense:

  • The client updates the AAAA record and the server updates the PTR record.
  • The server updates both records.

The reason is authority. A site may let a client manage its own AAAA record, or it may restrict that to the server so that clients cannot list arbitrary addresses or claim arbitrary names. The PTR record, however, is best managed by the server that allocates the address. A third case is also supported, where the client asks the server to do no updates, but the RFC presumes it to be rare.

Whether any client or server may update DNS at all is a matter of local administrative policy. The document does not require or propose any particular policy, and it applies only to DHCPv6 client and server processes.
sections.plainLanguage: There are two pages in the phone book: name-to-number and number-to-name. The helper always writes the second one. The computer or the helper can write the first, depending on the house rules.

sections.title: The Client FQDN Option and Its Flags
sections.content:
The option has code 39 (OPTION_CLIENT_FQDN) and a minimum length of 1 octet. It holds a one-octet flags field followed by the domain-name, so option-len is 1 plus the length of the name. It appears only in a message's options field and applies to all addresses of all IA_NA bindings in the transaction.

The flags field has three defined bits, and the remaining bits (MBZ) must be cleared by senders and ignored by receivers:

  • S: the client sets 1 to ask the server to update the AAAA record and 0 to ask it not to. In a reply, 1 means the server has taken responsibility for the AAAA update.
  • O: the server sets this to 1 when its S bit differs from the client's, meaning it overrode the client's preference. A client MUST set it to 0.
  • N: 1 means the server SHOULD NOT perform any DNS updates. A server sets it to say whether it will (0) or will not (1) update. If N is 1, S MUST be 0.

The domain name uses the DHCPv6 encoding from RFC 3315. A fully qualified name ends with the zero-length label. A partial name leaves that label off, which says the client knows only part of its name. A client can also leave the field empty if it wants the server to supply a name. Servers SHOULD send the complete FQDN, and client and server MUST NOT alter the field unless the FQDN has actually changed.
sections.plainLanguage: The option is a small note with three tick boxes and a name. The boxes say who writes what in the phone book, and the name can be whole, half, or left blank for the helper to fill in.

sections.title: Client Behavior
sections.content:
A client MUST include the option only in SOLICIT, REQUEST, RENEW or REBIND messages. If it expects the server to include the option in replies, it MUST also list it in the Option Request option. There are three things a client can ask for:

  • Client updates the AAAA record: S, O and N are all 0. Once configuration completes, the client MAY update unless the server set S to 1. If S is 1 the client SHOULD NOT update the name the server returned, though a client explicitly configured with an FQDN may ignore S if the returned name matches.
  • Server updates the AAAA record: S is 1, O and N are 0.
  • No server updates: N is 1, S and O are 0. The client MAY then do its own updates if the server also returns N as 1.

A client that delegates the update never hears whether it succeeded. It can query DNS, but can only infer success, because zone transfers or caches may lag. A client responsible for its AAAA record SHOULD delete it before sending RELEASE, or try to delete it if it cannot renew the address, and SHOULD try to notify an administrator if it fails. It SHOULD NOT update AAAA records for non-global-unicast or temporary addresses.
sections.plainLanguage: The computer picks one of three choices: I will write my own entry, you write it for me, or please write nothing. It cannot see whether the helper really wrote it, but it can look in the book to check.

sections.title: Server Behavior and TTLs
sections.content:
A server includes the option in ADVERTISE and REPLY only if the client sent it and asked for it in the Option Request option. It starts with S, O and N at 0, then sets N to 1 if the client asked for no updates and its configuration allows that. Otherwise it sets S to 1 if the client asked for that and policy allows, and sets O to 1 if its S differs from the client's. The server may use the client's name, change it, or substitute a different one.

The server SHOULD NOT update DNS if N is 1 in its reply, and SHOULD delete records it added earlier. Otherwise it MAY update the PTR record, and MAY update the AAAA record if S is 1. It MUST NOT start updates when it sends an ADVERTISE. It may finish updates before or after the REPLY, which means a name conflict could change the name between exchanges. When a binding ends through RELEASE, DECLINE, expiry or a zero valid lifetime, the server SHOULD delete the PTR record, and the AAAA record too if it was responsible.

For TTLs, records added for DHCP leases SHOULD be shorter than the initial lifetime: no more than 1/3 of the lifetime, but not less than 10 minutes. Administrators SHOULD be able to configure the values.
sections.plainLanguage: The helper reads the computer's note, decides what it is willing to do, and writes its own answer on the note. It cleans up its entries when the computer leaves, and makes entries that expire quickly so the book does not stay wrong for long.

sections.title: Conflicts, IANA and Security
sections.content:
The RFC does not say how to prevent name conflicts. It points out that conflicts cannot occur if only one updater holds the security token for a name, or if names are based on the bound address, and otherwise says a technique from RFC 4703 SHOULD be used. IANA assigned DHCPv6 option code 39.

Unauthenticated DNS updates can cause confusion through attack or misconfiguration, so administrators should be wary of allowing them on zones exposed to the global Internet. Clients and servers SHOULD use origin authentication such as Secure DNS Dynamic Update (RFC 3007). A server updating on a client's behalf SHOULD be sure of the name and of the client's identity, which it may not be without authentication in DHCPv6. Proper conflict resolution is called critical.
sections.plainLanguage: If anyone could scribble in the phone book, it would get confusing or be used for tricks. So the writer should prove who they are, and two computers should not get the same name.

fields.name: option-len
fields.desc: 1 plus the length of the domain name.

fields.name: flags
fields.desc: Flag bits MBZ, N, O and S used to negotiate who performs which updates.

fields.name: domain-name
fields.desc: Partial or fully qualified domain name, option-len minus 1 octets long (variable length).

items.label: Server updates AAAA
items.desc: Client: 1 asks the server to update the AAAA record. Server: 1 means it has taken that responsibility.

items.label: Override
items.desc: Server sets 1 if its S bit differs from the client's. Clients MUST send 0.

items.label: No server updates
items.desc: 1 means the server SHOULD NOT perform any DNS updates. If N is 1, S MUST be 0.
